title: Man's strength scared officer: In throes of rage, schizophrenic man lashed out at police: FATALITY INQUIRY
article: Raging psychiatric patient Kasim Cakmak was so strong as he battled three men trying to subdue him last spring that a police officer feared they'd be unable to control him.
"It was a scary situation,"
Const. John Tedeschini told a fatality inquiry Thursday.
"I have been in altercations before ... but there's nothing to compare with the strength he displayed and the duration of it."
He and another officer arrived around 2:30 p.m. last May 11 at the downtown mental health clinic, 9942 108th St., to transport the 37-year-old paranoid schizophrenic to Alberta Hospital Edmonton.
He'd been following women in the building, muttering to himself, yelling and acting aggressively, so a psychiatrist had declared him an involuntary patient who could be treated against his will.
But when police approached him with psychiatric nurse Mike Brohman, he went wild, thrashing, screaming and lashing out.
Tedeschini, six feet two inches tall and weighing more than 200 pounds (94 kg), testified it took all his might just to hold on to Cakmak's left arm as he vainly attempted to put on handcuffs.
"We were on the ground with him. He was on his stomach," said the nine-year police veteran, who paused several times to compose himself.
"I recall being physically lifted up off the ground ... part of my body was totally on his and he pushed me up and off."
He finally reached from behind as they stood struggling and gave Cakmak a one- or two-second blast of pepper spray in the face from 30 centimetres away.
It did nothing. The officer repeatedly smashed him in the temple with the base of his hand and his knee, but Cakmak still didn't react.
Tedeschini finally managed to get his hands behind his back and cuffed when the other officer shoved the tip of his baton into a pressure point behind Cakmak's left ear.
Tedeschini, who estimated the battle in a fourth-floor recreation room lasted six to nine minutes, said he suddenly felt the other man go limp as he fought to hold him face down on the floor.
They took off the cuffs and rolled him over, but witnesses said he was blue and didn't have a pulse.

Dr. Graeme Dowling, Alberta's chief medical examiner, has testified Cakmak died of excited delirium, a rare condition affecting primarily psychiatric patients and cocaine users in which they become so wildly agitated that an overpowering adrenalin rush stops their heart.
It's unclear what brings it on or how to treat it. Dowling, who doubted the pepper spray contributed to his death, has seen eight Alberta deaths from this condition in 16 years.
Cakmak moved to Canada in 1991 from Turkey, where medical files indicate he was tortured in prison.
There has also been evidence at the inquiry that he feared uniforms, but Tedeschini said he didn't take the fight personally.
"This is a sick man who needed help. I never felt he had something against me."
